definition: The practice of monitoring user activity across multiple websites to build detailed profiles of browsing behavior, interests, and preferences for advertising or analytics purposes.
metaDescription: Learn about cross site tracking - how companies monitor your browsing across websites to build detailed user profiles for advertising and analytics.
simpleExplanation: Cross site tracking is like having someone follow you from store to store, taking notes about what you look at and buy. Companies use various techniques to track your browsing across different websites, building a detailed picture of your interests and habits.
whyItMatters: This tracking can compromise your privacy by creating comprehensive profiles of your personal interests, habits, and behavior patterns. These profiles can be sold to advertisers, used to manipulate your choices, or potentially exposed in data breaches.
technicalDetail: Cross site tracking typically uses third-party cookies, pixel tracking, browser fingerprinting, and other techniques. Trackers embed code on multiple websites to collect data about user visits, clicks, and behavior patterns. This data is then aggregated across sites to create detailed user profiles for targeted advertising and analytics.

examples.explanation: You browse shoes on multiple shopping sites. Ad networks track these visits and start showing you shoe ads on news sites, social media, and other unrelated websites you visit.

You read articles about a medical condition on various health websites. Data brokers collect this information and may sell lists of people interested in health topics to insurance companies or pharmaceutical advertisers.
Social media platforms embed tracking pixels on news sites and blogs. Even if you don't interact with their content, they can track which articles you read and use this to target ads and content.
